why: A bitonic subsequence is fixed by its peak: an increasing subsequence ending at the peak times a decreasing one starting there. inc[i] = 1 + sum of inc[j] for j < i with arr[j] < arr[i] is counting DP, and a Fenwick tree indexed by value (only 200 values) makes that prefix sum O(log V), which is where this week's Fenwick tree comes in.
hints: Pick the peak of the subsequence. How do the left part and the right part depend on each other?
They are independent: count = (strictly increasing subsequences ending at i, at least 2 long) * (strictly decreasing subsequences starting at i, at least 2 long), summed over i.

inc[i] = 1 + sum of inc over earlier smaller values: a Fenwick tree keyed by value gives it in O(log V). Do the same right-to-left for dec. Answer = sum (inc[i] - 1) * (dec[i] - 1) mod 1e9+7. O(n log V).
pitfalls: Subtract the singleton from both sides; a pure increasing or pure decreasing sequence does not count.
Strict comparisons: equal values cannot be adjacent in the subsequence, so query values below v, not at most v.
Subsequences are counted by index set, so equal-looking sequences from different indices count separately.
Take the modulus during the Fenwick updates, not only at the end.
statement:
Given arr, count the subsequences (chosen by index, so two different index sets count separately even if their values look the same) that strictly increase to a peak and then strictly decrease, where both the rising part and the falling part have at least one step. So every such subsequence has length at least 3. Return the count modulo 10^9 + 7.

Worked example: arr = [1, 2, 3, 2, 1]. Group by the peak:

  • Peak 3 (index 2): the rising part ending at it is one of [1,3], [2,3], [1,2,3] (3 ways); the falling part is one of [3,2], [3,1], [3,2,1] (3 ways). 3 * 3 = 9.
  • Peak 2 at index 1: [1,2] then [2,1] using the last 1: 1 way.
  • Peak 2 at index 3: [1,2] then [2,1]: 1 way.
  • Total 9 + 1 + 1 = 11.
